doc.title: Byron Stripling interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 25, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Police stops, fear while walking, and artists speaking out
summary: Stripling tells of a traffic stop while driving to the International Trumpet Guild, his wife's fear after George Floyd, and jazz musicians' long experience.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: your response? So one thing about artists is we do have feelings. And we express them generally through music but we also — it’s necessary for us to take a stand verbally and to language through our art but also verbally. So “shut up and dribble” that’s slave stuff. Right? When somebody tells you, “Yeah you guys get beaten when you get stopped by the police, that’s ‘cause you’re not acting like you’re supposed to act.” You know how they want you to act? Like a slave. “Yessir boss, I’s sorry. Here’s my license.” That’s the attitude that they would want you to do. I was stopped with a dear friend, my dear friend who is white. We were driving to the International Trumpet Guild in Texas. He’s from Texas. He was driving. Going to see the Trumpet Guild. He was going too fast. We knew it, we wanted to get there and go see the — and I said I knew it was going to happen. And I won’t say his name because he’d be embarrassed for me telling the story. But we laugh about it together. The policeman pulls us both over. I was just like okay, just be cool, just be cool. He goes, “No, no, I’ll be right back.” And he jumped out of the car and ran back to the policeman. I’m like, “What are you doing? What are you doing you know?” So I’m sitting there on pins and needles. I mean this is probably twenty years ago, which wouldn’t have mattered racially on my case. So he ran back and he was back in about two minutes. And I said — and he goes “Okay we’re good, let’s go.” I said, “What just happened?” you know, as we were driving away. He said, “I told him we were in a hurry.” Great. I mean I couldn’t have done that. So what all of this stuff, and I apologize for talking about this stuff but I think it’s where the pandemic has brought us. What all of this stuff brings up is me. I don’t have a real take on being affected by racism in a way a lot of other people have. But I do know that I’ve made a goal to walk every day of the pandemic. I have no excuses, Monk. There was nothing I could say, oh I don’t have time, right. Exactly. So I said I’ve got to walk every day. And I’ve only missed like four days, because I got busy with stuff. So that’s been a pretty good record. Problem was the more uprising and my wife and I watched George Floyd get assassinated on TV by somebody’s knee. My wife said I don’t want you to walk unless I’m with you. I don’t think that’s a reality that most people have to think about, but I do as a black man. And it’s nothing I want people to feel sorry for me or I just think it’s something that exists for me, that every time when I do walk and there happens to be a police car coming by, I’m very nervous about it. And that’s a reality for me. And I think I need to be. And I will be respectful if I get stopped, but I’ve seen videos that tells me that that doesn’t matter. So the pandemic has brought up all these things which were always there simmering under there. And us jazz musicians from Louis Armstrong to Coltrane to Don Cherry and Ornette and from the current day guys and Wynton and all those guys, we’ve all experienced that and we’ve all tried to sort of dampen it down with our music. But there’s always those people that are happy — yeah you can dance. You can play football.
You can play your horn. Sing for me boy. But they don’t want you to have an opinion about something. And I’ve got opinions. And my opinions aren’t wrong.
